claims.text: Rapid solidification during synthesis prevents elemental segregation in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid solidification ensures formation of a single-phase, homogeneously mixed alloy.
A homogeneously mixed alloy presents a uniformly distributed array of catalytically active sites.
Rapidly solidified nanoparticles will have better catalytic performance than conventionally slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Slow cooling may cause elemental segregation or phase separation in noble metal–based HEA nanoparticles.
A high cooling rate can lock in a random, high-entropy alloy state.
Rapid cooling minimizes the time available for atomic diffusion and segregation.
Suppressed diffusion during rapid cooling preserves a single-phase, disordered alloy structure.
Preserving the disordered alloy state produces a homogeneous surface composition with evenly distributed catalytic sites.
Slow cooling allows local elemental clustering.
Local elemental clustering can reduce the effective density of active sites.
A reduction in effective active-site density impairs catalytic efficiency.
Rapidly solidified nanoparticles will exhibit greater elemental uniformity than composition-matched slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly solidified nanoparticles will exhibit higher reaction rates or turnover frequencies than composition-matched slow-cooled nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for nanoscale noble metal–based HEA catalysts in reactions conducted at temperatures no greater than approximately 600 °C.
